title: Shiva Intercedes; Vana Dances for Boons
story:
The war for Sonitpura was over, but its king was not yet safe. Vana, who had fought with a thousand arms, stood weaponless with two, and above him Krishna's discus still circled in the air, bright as a second sun over the ruined field. Every soldier knew what came next: the Yadavas, Krishna's kinsmen, waited to see the war finished, and the demons who had fought beside Vana had already turned away. It was then that Shiva spoke.

"I have promised this king my protection," said Shiva, coming forward through the dust and smoke, with Nandi the bull at his side. "Long ago I gave Vana my word that I would shield him. He has worshipped me, and I have not forgotten it, and I will not see my promise broken. Desist, Krishna. Let him live."

Krishna looked at the god who had watched the whole war from the heights. He had sworn to the goddess Kottavi that Vana would lose his thousand arms but keep his life, and that vow was already kept — only two arms remained. The life itself was another matter, and a word from Shiva was not a small thing. "I withdraw my discus," he said. "At your request, Vana will live."

The discus returned to his hand, and the light of it went out of the air. A murmur ran through both armies — wonder from the Yadavas, and from the demons a hope they had not dared to feel. Vana stood where his chariot had been shattered, looking at his two empty hands as if he had never seen them before. He had entered this battle with a thousand weapons and the pride of a king who thought himself beyond defeat. He was leaving it with nothing but his life, and even that was a gift.

Then Nandi, Shiva's bull, came close to him. "Dance," Nandi said. "Dance before the lord."

And the two-armed king of Sonitpura danced. He danced on the field where he had fought, turning slowly at first, then with a strange gathering grace, his body moving through gestures his hands could no longer make, as if the dance itself remembered the thousand arms that had once made it. There was nothing comic in it. The armies watched in silence; the gods watching from above grew still; and Shiva watched, and was pleased.

"I am pleased with you, Vana," said the god. "Ask a boon of me."

What Vana asked for, the tellings do not set down; they record only that Shiva was pleased and granted it. But this much is certain: the king who had marched to war as an enemy of the Yadavas left the field as Mahakala, chief of the Pramathas — first among the spirit hosts that serve Shiva — and went from there in the god's own company, bound not to a throne but to the service of the one who had spared him. Where he had once counted his power in arms and weapons, he now counted it in the favour of Shiva.

Behind him, the field fell quiet in the strange calm that follows an ending. The armies gathered their fallen and their wounded, and the dust settled over the thousand arms that lay like a felled forest between them. Of the king who had raised them, nothing was left but a dancer and a devotee — and a name that would be spoken with respect in the courts of heaven.
reflection: The armless king dancing before Shiva is the heart of the episode: stripped of everything he had fought with, Vana finds favour in the one thing left to him, devotion. What the battlefield could never give him — a place of honour — the dance does.
next_story_tease: But the day's work was not done: Vana's celestial cows still grazed in Varuna's keeping, and Krishna meant to have them.
hero_scene: The two-armed Vana dancing before Shiva on the battlefield, his body mid-gesture, Shiva watching with pleasure beside Nandi the bull, while Krishna's discus rests in his hand and the armies look on in silence.
